extracted.intended_audience: general readers and abolitionist activists (19th-century lecturing/public-speaking context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and embedded standards for narrating personal bondage and conducting abolitionist public speaking, as illustrated in an autobiographical lecture/travel narrative. Emphasizes authenticity, audience management, safety, rhetorical balance, and strategic compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide factual details to establish authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Write out the leading facts connected with your experience in slavery, giving names of persons, places, and dates—thus putting it in the power of any who doubted to ascertain the truth or falsehood of your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass recounts that after audience doubts rose, he was 'induced to write out the leading facts' with specific names/places/dates to dispel imposture claims. This is presented as an explicit method to verify a personal narrative and counter skepticism; but publishing such facts can create personal risk (see safety/privacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with concrete narration ('Give us the facts')
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences initially demanded narrations of personal experience rather than abstract argument—'Let us have the facts' / 'Give us the facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early talks were 'almost exclusively made up of narrations' because listeners wanted concrete testimony. Use vivid, circumstantial storytelling early to engage audiences who ask for facts rather than philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance narration with denunciation and moral argument
rubrics_metrics.description: While narration is necessary, the speaker/writer should also 'denounce' wrongs—moral indignation may be required and can be more than mere recitation of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass felt 'it did not entirely satisfy me to narrate wrongs; I felt like denouncing them.' He notes that moral denunciation can be compelling but may conflict with expectations for straightforward testimony; choose tone based on purpose and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolve content to avoid mechanical repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repeating the same story month after month; repetition becomes 'a task altogether too mechanical' and reduces the speaker's engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As one grows intellectually, vary speeches—add new views, broaden from narration to analysis. Repetition is an anti-pattern; audiences want fresh perspective even on familiar facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt manner of speech for credibility ('plantation manner' advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friends advised: 'Better have a little of the plantation manner of speech than not; 'tis not best that you seem too learned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust some stylistic markers to meet audience expectations and preserve credibility (e.g., dialectal cues or mannerisms when appropriate). But balance this with 'Be yourself'—avoid affectation that undermines authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be yourself and tell your story
rubrics_metrics.description: Advisors also counseled: 'Be yourself' and 'tell your story.' Authentic voice matters as much as calculated performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity builds trust; do not adopt an entirely performative persona that contradicts your genuine perspective. Use temperament and voice that feel true to you while still communicating clearly to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage safety and privacy when publishing personal facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Withhold or delay revealing identifying details (former name, master's name, state/county) until prudent—initially withheld to prevent recapture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass withheld key details early to prevent his master from learning his whereabouts. Publishing fuller factual detail later dispels skepticism but increases personal risk (could prompt attempts at recapture). Weigh verification value against safety consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and directly address audience skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience skepticism (e.g., 'He don't tell us where he came from... he is educated') must be countered—either by narrative choices or by providing verifiable facts to 'dispel all doubt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize common doubts (appearance, education, omission of details) and decide whether to rebut by producing documentary detail, testimony, or rhetorical framing to preempt accusations of imposture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use incidents and controversy to increase public attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Public incidents (e.g., the mob on board the 'Cambria') and reactions of opponents may generate press and public interest, effectively amplifying your message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversy can be leveraged: enemies' attempts to silence you can validate your importance and draw audiences. Be prepared for both risks (threats, violence) and benefits (wider platform).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame appeals on universal human brotherhood (avoid national antagonism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Address audiences (even foreign ones) on the high ground of human brotherhood—'Slavery is a crime... against God, and all the members of the human family'—and avoid presenting one nation entirely against another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When speaking to international publics, emphasize shared humanity and moral principles rather than national critique; Douglass notes he never addressed Englishmen 'as against Americans' but appealed for aid in humanity's name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept strategic, pragmatic compromises for larger aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic decisions (e.g., accepting purchase of freedom) may conflict with ideological purity but be warranted by pragmatic considerations and greater goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass recounts critics who saw his ransom as conceding property-in-man principles; he defends it as a ransom that enabled continued work for emancipation. Evaluate trade-offs between principle and capacity to act.
